description_full: Granite Construction Incorporated provides infrastructure solutions for public and private clients in the United States. It operates through Construction and Materials segments. The Construction segment engages in the construction and rehabilitation of roads, pavement preservation, bridges, rail lines, airports, marine ports, dams, reservoirs, aqueducts, infrastructure, and site development for use by the public and water-related construction for municipal agencies, commercial water suppliers, industrial facilities, and energy companies; and construction of various complex projects, including infrastructure and site development, mining, public safety, tunnel, solar, battery storage, and power related projects. The Materials segment produces and delivers aggregates, asphalt concrete, liquid asphalt, and recycled materials for internal use in construction projects and sale to third parties. It also provides site preparation, mining, and infrastructure services for railways, residential development, energy development, and commercial and industrial sites; produces construction materials; and provides construction management professional services, as well as owns and leases aggregate reserves and processing plants. The company serves federal agencies, state departments of transportation, local transit authorities, county and city public works departments, school districts and developers, utilities, contractors, landscapers, manufacturers of products requiring aggregate materials, retailers, homeowners, farmers, brokers, and private owners of industrial, commercial, and residential sites. Granite Construction Incorporated was incorporated in 1922 and is headquartered in Watsonville, California.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 2K people. Revenue per employee of $1.8M ranks in the top quartile among Industrials peers, improving at 6%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $132K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $16K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: Granite Construction Incorporat is a mid-cap industrials business with a $5.3B market cap on $4.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 8% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 11% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $331M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.43× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.7× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 6.0×.
Shareholder yield is only 1.3%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.58x).
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 22% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 26% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 36% and a beta of 0.98, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.10 vs 5y 0.97), so read it loosely.
About $64.7M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 65% in the 2020 crash, 35% in the 2022 bear market and 45% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $44.66 (margin of safety -170%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 4%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $31.56 to $63.10 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 14.3 vs 23.3 and P/FCF 16.1 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 22% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $173 on average, 44% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.3%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 2.30).
It runs a 11% gross margin and converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.43x.
ROE of 16% is amplified by 3.4x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.9% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.7x net debt to EBITDA ($600.2M of cash against $1.3B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.0x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 10.3% over 3 years, 4.4% over 5 years and 6.4% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 13.5% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.12 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 93% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 9%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 3.1% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 11, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.9%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 4 purchases and 12 sales over the past year, net $7.5M sold.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.3% (0.9% in buybacks and 0.4% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 15.1% of the float, 6.2 days to cover.
people: With about 2,500 employees, each generates about $1.8M of revenue, 4.8x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 6.3% a year.
That works out to $132K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.7M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
